text: pulmonary aspergillosis (CNPA or subacute invasive pulmonary aspergillosis)17 is a subacute infection seen in patients with an underlying lung disease or systemic risk factors for immunosuppression. Various antifungals have been tried in the treatment of CNPA. Case reports have shown amphotericin B to be successful in about 50% of the patients and clinical benefit has also been achieved with intracavitary amphotericin B. Flucytosine has been used with or without amphotericin B. Itracona- zole has a reported success rate of 70 to 90%. Treatment needs to be prolonged, so oral antifungals are preferred to parenteral antifungal therapy. Current evidence supports the use of itraconazole, with voriconazole and possibly also posaconazole as alternatives, for the treatment of CN- PA.11 Aspergillosis of the eye, like other fungal eye infections, is difficult to treat; antifungals are generally not well ab- sorbed after topical application and infections extending into the vitreous or anterior chamber require subconjuncti- val, intra-ocular, and/or systemic treatment. Systemic treatment is necessary for ocular manifestations of dissem- inated disease. Intravenous and intravitreal amphotericin B are recommended for the treatment of Aspergillus endo- phthalmitis; intravitreal or systemic voriconazole may be given as an alternative. For the management of Aspergillus keratitis topical antifungal therapy plus systemic antifun- gal therapy with either amphotericin B, voriconazole, or itraconazole is recommended.11 For superficial eye infec- tions a number of drugs including natamycin, amphoter- icin B, azoles, and sulfadiazine silver have been applied topically alone or as an adjunct to systemic therapy.
